subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Organ Donation Defaults
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Organ Donation Defaults.

hook.text: Austria: 99% donor rate. Germany: 12%. One is opt-out, the other opt-in. Same culture, different default.

buildup.text: People have strong feelings about donating organs. But they rarely act on them. The default does the acting.

discovery.text: The decision isn't really about organs. It's about effort, discomfort, and the status quo. Defaults absorb all three.

twist.text: Some ethicists argue mandated choice is better: force everyone to decide.

climax.text: The organ donation gap proves that policy design matters more than public opinion. Most people support donation.

punchline.text: Intent without a default stays intent.

quiz.question: Why does Austria have a 99% organ donor rate?
options: Organ donation is the default; you must opt out to refuse

details.summary: Organ donation defaults demonstrate the extraordinary power of opt-in versus opt-out framing. Countries with opt-out donation see over 90 percent consent rates while countries with opt-in see around 15 percent, despite similar attitudes toward donation in both populations.
details.whyItMatters: The organ donation default gap is the single most compelling illustration of default power. Thousands of lives that could be saved are lost because the default in many countries requires active consent.
takeaways: Opt-out countries have over 90 percent organ donation consent; opt-in countries have about 15 percent
The difference is not explained by cultural attitudes toward donation
Switching the default from opt-in to opt-out would save thousands of lives per year

faq.question: Why do organ donation rates differ so dramatically between countries?
faq.answer: The difference is almost entirely explained by the default. In opt-in countries, people must actively register. In opt-out countries, everyone is a donor unless they actively opt out. Since most people do not change defaults, the registration rate mirrors the default.

faq.question: Are there ethical concerns with opt-out organ donation?
faq.answer: Critics argue presumed consent does not equal informed consent. Supporters argue the default never prevents opting out and the stakes in lives saved are enormous. Most adopt a soft opt-out approach that still checks with families before proceeding.
